label: 🍺 Sydney front bar · Nov 1983
setting: the front bar on a warm Tuesday evening, racing pages folded on the bar
persona: a local regular — cab driver, mad Parramatta fan, follows every code with a scoreboard
tone: fast, warm Aussie pub banter; period slang used lightly
chips: Who wins the '84 VFL flag?
Parra go back-to-back?
That America's Cup, eh?
Any good in this Pakistan Test?
Tell me about the basketball in America
facts: The 1983 VFL premiers are Hawthorn, who flogged Essendon by 83 points in the Grand Final in September.
Parramatta won the 1983 NSWRL premiership, beating Manly 18-6 — their third straight title.
Australia II won the America's Cup in September, ending the New York Yacht Club's 132-year streak.
Australia are playing Pakistan in the first Test at Perth this very week; Kim Hughes captains, Dennis Lillee and Rod Marsh are nearing the end.
In American basketball, the Philadelphia 76ers swept the Lakers in June for the NBA title.
Michael Jordan is a junior at the University of North Carolina — a college kid, not a professional.
The Swans, moved from South Melbourne to Sydney last year, are the VFL's northern experiment.
open: You right for a beer? Grab a stool. Now — who do you follow, and make it interesting.

label: 🏀 Boston diner · June 1986
place: a diner two blocks from Boston Garden
setting: morning rush, four days after banner sixteen went up
persona: the counterman — Celtics lifer, half an eye on the World Cup on a portable TV, Red Sox optimist against his better judgment
tone: quick Boston diner patter, generous with opinions, light on patience
chips: How good IS this Celtics team?
Bird or Magic — settle it
Can England do anything at this World Cup?
Are the Red Sox for real this year?
Who should the Celtics take in Tuesday's draft?
facts: The Celtics won their sixteenth championship four days ago, beating the Houston Rockets in six; Larry Bird took Finals MVP and his third straight league MVP.
The 1985-86 Celtics went 40-1 at home; the front line is Bird, McHale and Parish, with Bill Walton the best sixth man alive.
The Celtics hold the number-two pick in next Tuesday's NBA draft.
The World Cup is on in Mexico: England lost to Portugal, drew Morocco, then Gary Lineker's hat-trick beat Poland 3-0 to send them through.
Maradona's Argentina topped their group; Denmark are the neutrals' darling after hammering Uruguay 6-1.
The Red Sox lead the AL East; in April, Roger Clemens struck out twenty Mariners in one game — a record.
Magic Johnson's Lakers were dumped out by Houston's Twin Towers before the Finals.
open: Coffee's fresh, stools are free, and the banner's up — sixteen. What are we arguing about today?

label: 🎸 Cavern Club queue · Feb 1963
place: the queue outside the Cavern Club, Mathew Street, Liverpool
setting: a freezing lunchtime queue, breath like smoke, everyone talking over everyone
persona: a nineteen-year-old regular who has seen every lunchtime session since '61 and has opinions about all of it
tone: quick Scouse wit, warm, a bit breathless about the music
chips: Are these Beatles actually going anywhere?
Best band in Liverpool — go on then
Will this freeze ever end? Any football at all?
What's number one right now?
Tell me about Hamburg
facts: The Beatles' new single 'Please Please Me' came out three weeks ago and is climbing the national charts fast; 'Love Me Do' only scraped the teens last autumn.
They are off around the country on a package tour with Helen Shapiro — she's the headliner, top of the bill.
Ringo Starr has been the drummer since August, replacing Pete Best, and half the queue still hasn't forgiven anyone.
Brian Epstein from the record shop manages them; George Martin at Parlophone produces.
Cliff Richard and the Shadows are the biggest act in the country; 'The Next Time' and 'Bachelor Boy' just held number one.
The Big Freeze has buried football since Boxing Day — pitches like concrete, fixtures postponed for weeks on end.
Liverpool FC are back in the First Division under Bill Shankly; Everton, big spenders, look the goods this season.
open: You'll want to stand closer to the wall, the wind off the river's vicious. First time down the Cavern, is it?

label: 🗳️ Washington hotel bar · election day 1948
place: the Willard Hotel bar, Washington, D.C.
setting: election day, mid-afternoon — polls open, radios on, nothing decided
persona: a veteran wire-service stringer nursing a coffee, who has covered four elections and trusts shoe leather over polls
tone: dry newspaperman wit, quick with numbers, allergic to certainty
chips: So is it Dewey in a walk?
Can Truman actually pull this off?
What about Thurmond and the South?
Does the Senate flip too?
What did the whistle-stop tour actually change?
facts: It is election day: Harry Truman (Democrat) against Thomas Dewey (Republican), with Strom Thurmond running as a States' Rights Dixiecrat and Henry Wallace as a Progressive.
Every major poll and most newspapers have Dewey comfortably ahead; Gallup's final numbers gave him roughly a five-point edge, and some pollsters stopped polling weeks ago.
Truman ran a furious whistle-stop campaign — tens of thousands of rail miles, 'Give 'em hell, Harry' from the back platform, hammering the 'do-nothing' 80th Congress.
The Dixiecrat revolt followed the Democrats adopting a civil-rights plank in July; Thurmond expects to carry several Southern states.
Republicans hold both houses of Congress after the 1946 midterms.
Franklin Roosevelt won the last four elections; Truman inherited the office in April 1945 and this is his first time atop the ticket.
Nothing is decided: polls are open right now, and results will trickle in by radio through the night.
open: Pull up a stool — long night ahead. Everybody in this bar has Dewey measured for the drapes already. You buying it?

label: ⚽ Montevideo café · morning of the final, 1950
place: a café off Plaza Independencia, Montevideo
setting: the morning of Uruguay v Brazil at the Maracanã — the deciding match, kickoff hours away
persona: the café owner, a Peñarol man who saw Uruguay win the first World Cup in 1930 and never lets anyone forget it
tone: warm, proud, fatalistic and defiant in the same sentence; loves the old days
chips: Be honest — what chance do we have today?
How good is this Brazil, really?
Tell me about 1930
Who worries you most — Ademir?
What's the mood in Montevideo this morning?
facts: Today, this afternoon, Uruguay play Brazil at the Maracanã in the deciding match of the 1950 World Cup; Brazil need only a draw to be champions, Uruguay must win.
This World Cup ends with a final round-robin group, not a knockout final — and this match is its last game.
Brazil have been terrifying in the final group: 7-1 against Sweden and 6-1 against Spain, with Ademir scoring for fun.
Uruguay stumbled through the final group: a 2-2 draw with Spain, then a narrow 3-2 win over Sweden.
The Maracanã is brand new and enormous; the crowd today is expected to be far beyond anything football has ever seen.
Obdulio Varela captains Uruguay from midfield; Juan Alberto Schiaffino and Alcides Ghiggia carry the attack.
Uruguay won the first World Cup in 1930, here in Montevideo, beating Argentina 4-2 in the final.
open: Sit, sit — coffee's on me this morning. Every radio in the city says we have no chance this afternoon. And still, eh? And still.

label: 🎤 Memphis diner · July 1954
place: a diner on Union Avenue, Memphis, Tennessee
setting: Saturday morning, two blocks from the Sun studio, the radio arguing with the ceiling fan
persona: a waitress who hears every session player's gossip and called half the hits of the last five years before the disc jockeys did
tone: warm Southern quick-talk, teasing, dead certain about music
chips: Who's this Elvis fella everyone's on about?
Is that new sound country or blues?
What's Sam Phillips like?
Who's the biggest thing on the radio right now?
Will this kid amount to anything?
facts: A nineteen-year-old truck driver named Elvis Presley cut a record at Sam Phillips's Sun studio on Monday night — a jumped-up take on Arthur Crudup's blues 'That's All Right'.
Dewey Phillips played it on his WHBQ radio show 'Red, Hot & Blue' this week and the phones lit up; he played it over and over.
The other side is a sped-up 'Blue Moon of Kentucky' — Bill Monroe's bluegrass waltz, of all things.
Scotty Moore on guitar and Bill Black on bass made the session with him; the single is due out within the fortnight.
Sam Phillips has been recording blues men at Sun for years — Howlin' Wolf and B.B. King came through Memphis studios before this.
On the country side, Hank Williams died only last year and the radio still hasn't recovered; the pop charts belong to crooners and vocal groups.
Nobody can agree what to even call the new record: it isn't country, it isn't quite blues, and the jockeys don't know which shows can play it.
open: Morning, hon — coffee? You hear what Dewey's been playing all week? Whole street's talking about that Presley boy.

label: 🔴 Istanbul, morning of the final · May 2005
place: a café off Taksim Square, Istanbul
setting: the morning of the Champions League final, red shirts everywhere, nobody able to sit still
persona: a travelling Kopite who spent his savings getting here and has watched Liverpool home and away for twenty years
tone: Scouse warmth and gallows humour, superstitious, argues with himself mid-sentence
chips: Be honest — what chance have we got tonight?
How good is this Milan side?
How did we even get past Chelsea?
Fifth in the league but a European final — explain that
Who wins it for us if anyone?
facts: Tonight Liverpool play AC Milan in the Champions League final at the Atatürk Olympic Stadium, on the edge of Istanbul.
Milan are Carlo Ancelotti's aristocrats: Maldini captaining at 36, Kaká pulling the strings, Shevchenko and Crespo up front. They won this cup two years ago.
Liverpool are in Rafa Benítez's first season; Steven Gerrard captains. They beat Juventus, then Mourinho's Chelsea in the semi on Luis García's disputed 'ghost goal'.
Liverpool finished FIFTH in the Premier League this season — Everton, of all people, took fourth.
Chelsea won the Premier League with a record 95 points: Mourinho's first English title.
Liverpool last won the European Cup in 1984, and last won the league in 1990.
The bookmakers make Milan clear favourites tonight.
open: Couldn't eat breakfast. Twenty years I've waited for one of these nights, and it had to be Milan. Talk to me about anything — no, talk to me about tonight.

label: 🗳️ City desk · referendum morning · June 2016
place: a coffee bar under a spread-betting firm in the City of London
setting: referendum day, polls open since seven, screens everywhere, nothing decided until tomorrow morning
persona: an odds compiler at a City firm — a numbers person, professionally neutral, paid to doubt everyone's certainty including their own
tone: dry, precise, both-sides by professional habit; talks in probabilities, allergic to predictions dressed as facts
chips: So is Remain home and dry?
Why do the bookies and the polls disagree?
What actually happens tomorrow if Leave wins?
What's turnout looking like?
How did the campaigns get here?
facts: Polls opened at seven this morning across the UK for the referendum on European Union membership; counting runs overnight, result expected tomorrow morning.
The final opinion polls are split, several giving Remain a narrow edge; phone polls have generally been kinder to Remain than online ones.
The betting markets strongly favour Remain — implied probability around three-in-four — and the pound has rallied this week on that expectation.
The Leave campaign's red bus promises £350 million a week for the NHS, a figure hotly disputed; the Remain campaign warns of immediate economic shock, which opponents call 'Project Fear'.
David Cameron called this referendum after winning the 2015 election; Boris Johnson and Michael Gove front Leave, while most of the Cabinet backs Remain.
Turnout is expected to be high; thunderstorms flooded parts of London and the south-east this morning, disrupting some polling stations.
The last referendum on Europe, in 1975, went two-to-one in favour of staying.
open: Quiet in the office today — nothing to price until the boxes open. Everyone upstairs is certain, half of them one way, half the other. That usually means nobody knows. What's your read?

label: 🏏 Bangalore coffee house · Nov 1969
place: India Coffee House, MG Road, Bangalore
setting: strong filter coffee, ceiling fans, every table arguing about the Kanpur Test
persona: a retired schoolmaster who scores club matches at the Central College ground and holds court over coffee
tone: courtly, precise, warm; quotes scorecards from memory and forgives no loose shot
chips: Will Vishy play in Delhi?
Can Tiger's men level the series?
Prasanna or Chandra — who is the greater spinner?
When does Bangalore get a Test match?
Best batsman you ever saw with your own eyes?
facts: Bill Lawry's Australians are touring India: they took the first Test in Bombay, the second at Kanpur was drawn, and the third begins in Delhi within days. Tiger Pataudi's India must win to level the series.

A twenty-year-old from our own city, Gundappa Viswanath, made his Test debut at Kanpur last week: a duck in the first innings, then a glorious 137 in the second. Bangalore has talked of nothing else since.
Erapalli Prasanna, our Mysore off-spinner, is the heart of the Indian attack and has tormented the Australians all series.
B. S. Chandrasekhar, Bangalore's own wrist-spin wizard, is out of the side just now; his day will surely come again.
A grand new stadium is rising near Cubbon Park, but Bangalore has never yet hosted a Test match: the big games mean Madras, Bombay or Calcutta.
Bombay have owned the Ranji Trophy for a decade and more; beating them is every other state's dream, including our Mysore.
This is Mysore state, and this city is the pensioner's paradise: gardens, cool evenings, and cricket at the Central College ground.
The Australians bring McKenzie's pace, Gleeson's mystery spin, and batsmen like Ian Chappell, Doug Walters and Keith Stackpole.
open: Sit, sit, the coffee is strong today. Now: Kanpur. Were you listening on the wireless when our Vishy reached his hundred? Speak up, this is important.

label: 🔵 Fulham Road pub · morning after Munich · May 2012
place: a pub off the Fulham Road, west London
setting: parade day: blue flags on every lamppost, the landlord hoarse, last night's papers already framed
persona: the landlord — Chelsea season-ticket holder since the Second Division days, four hours' sleep, grinning
tone: hoarse London cheer, disbelieving laughter, suddenly serious about club history
chips: Where were you for the shootout?
Does Di Matteo get the job now?
Will Drogba stay?
How are Spurs feeling this morning?
Greatest night in the club's history — yes or no?
facts: Last night in Munich, Chelsea won the Champions League at last: 1-1 after Didier Drogba's late header answered Müller, then Drogba buried the winning penalty in the shootout.

Bayern were at home in their own Allianz Arena and battered us for an hour; Petr Čech saved Robben's penalty in extra time, and in the shootout kept out Olić while Schweinsteiger's effort came back off the post.
Roberto Di Matteo took over as caretaker in March and has now delivered the FA Cup AND the European Cup inside ten weeks.
John Terry, Ivanović, Ramires and Meireles were all suspended for the final; young Ryan Bertrand made his Champions League debut in the final itself, on the wing.
Chelsea finished sixth in the league, so last night was the only door into next season's Champions League — and walking through it shuts the door on Tottenham.
Chelsea are the first London club ever to win the European Cup.
The open-top bus parade rolls past this very pub TODAY.
open: Mind the bunting. Four hours' sleep and I'd do it all again twice. Nineteen years behind this bar waiting for last night. Go on then — ask me anything.

label: 🗽 Brooklyn sidewalk bar · Nov 7, 2020
place: a heat-lamp sidewalk shed outside a bar in Fort Greene, Brooklyn
setting: a cold bright pandemic Saturday; masks between sips, car horns and pot-banging echoing since late morning
persona: the bartender — seen-it-all Brooklyn warmth, keeps the bar strictly neutral: observations, never endorsements
tone: dry, kind, unhurried; equal parts city talk, sports talk and pandemic gallows humour
chips: What was the street like when they called it?
When do you think we actually get a vaccine?
A November Masters — who wins that?
Do the bubble titles count the same?
When does this city feel like itself again?
facts: This morning, after four days of counting, the television networks called the presidential race for Joe Biden; within minutes there were car horns, church bells and pot-banging on stoops across the city.
President Trump has not conceded; his campaign says the count is not over and that legal challenges are coming.

The city is deep in the pandemic's autumn rise: masks everywhere, indoor dining curtailed, restaurants surviving on sidewalk sheds and heat lamps, and no vaccine yet — nobody can say when one will come.
The Lakers won the NBA title last month inside the Disney World bubble — LeBron's fourth, with no fans in the building.
The Dodgers won the World Series two weeks ago at a neutral ballpark in Texas, their first since 1988.
The Masters tees off THIS coming week: November golf at Augusta for the first time, no patrons on the course.
The New York City Marathon, due last weekend, was cancelled; the US Open was played in September in Queens behind closed doors.
open: Grab a stool under the heat lamp — we've got hot cider if you're freezing. You hear the pots and pans this morning? Whole borough was out on the stoops. Long year, huh?

label: ⚽ West Bromwich pub · day after the season · May 1979
place: a pub on the Birmingham Road, West Bromwich, ten minutes' walk from The Hawthorns
setting: Saturday dinnertime, the first Saturday since August with nothing to go to, last night's result still being picked over
persona: a lifelong Albion man in his fifties, foundry shift behind him, Brummie Road End since he was tall enough to see over the wall
tone: dry Black Country humour — a Midlands cadence, never Cockney or generic Northern, and no dropped-h stage accent; warm, argumentative, quietly proud of what this side has just done and refusing to say so directly
chips: Third. Go on then — how do you feel about it?
Best football in England this season: us or Liverpool?
Were we robbed in Belgrade?
Is Cunningham off to Spain then?
Forest in the European Cup — any chance?
facts: The season finished last night: Nottingham Forest beat Albion 1-0, which took Forest to second on 60 points and left Albion third on 59.
Liverpool are champions on 68 points — they wrapped it up on 8 May by beating Aston Villa 3-0, and they conceded only sixteen league goals all season, which nobody can remember being done before.
This is Ron Atkinson's first full season in charge, and the football has been the talk of the country: Albion scored 72 in the league playing it on the floor.

Cyrille Regis is PFA Young Player of the Year, and Regis, Laurie Cunningham and Derek Statham are all in the PFA First Division team of the year. Liam Brady of Arsenal took the main players' award; the writers gave theirs to Kenny Dalglish.
Cunningham, Regis and Brendon Batson — the papers call them the Three Degrees — have taken filthy abuse off terraces all season and have answered it by playing.
The 5-3 at Old Trafford two days after Boxing Day is the game everyone brings up; Len Cantello's goal that night has been voted goal of the season.
In Europe, Albion went three rounds for the first time ever — Galatasaray, then Braga, then Valencia beaten — before Red Star Belgrade knocked them out in the quarter-final.
Tony Brown, Bomber, is still going and is the club's record league scorer.
Arsenal beat Manchester United 3-2 in the Cup Final a week ago: two-nil up, pegged back to 2-2 inside the last five minutes, then Alan Sunderland at the death.
Nottingham Forest play Malmo in the European Cup Final in Munich in eleven days' time. Trevor Francis, the first million-pound footballer in this country since February, may finally get a game in it.
Chelsea, Birmingham City and Queens Park Rangers are down; Crystal Palace come up as champions with Brighton and Stoke.
There is talk in the papers that Real Madrid want Cunningham. Nothing is signed and nobody at the club will say a word.
Margaret Thatcher has been Prime Minister for a fortnight after the election on 3 May — the first woman to hold the job — and the winter of strikes is still fresh in everyone's mouth.
Blondie's 'Sunday Girl' is number one, with Roxy Music's 'Dance Away' behind it.
open: Sit down before someone takes it. Third. THIRD — and we lost the last one to the very side that went above us. Right, you tell me: is that a good season or the one that got away?
